note: Attacker-controlled HPACK input supplies a name-length varint with many 0xff continuation bytes. Each iteration increments shift by 7; after 5 continuation bytes shift=35, so the left shift of a 32-bit unsigned int is undefined behavior (shift exponent 35, then 63, confirmed by UBSan).
The undefined shifts wrap the accumulated value modulo 2^32, producing a truncated 32-bit length that no longer reflects the number of bytes actually consumed from the input.
The truncated nlen is accepted as the header name length because the check len < nlen passes for the small wrapped value, while raw has already advanced past all the continuation bytes.
The name ist is built from the wrong input offset with the truncated length, desynchronizing the decoder from the actual HPACK stream.
The value length is decoded from the desynchronized position; a second oversized varint again triggers the undefined shift in get_var_int, yielding another truncated length.
The value ist is built from the wrong offset with the truncated length, further corrupting the decoded header fields.
The corrupted name/value pairs are stored into the output header list, propagating the attacker-controlled truncated lengths into the caller.
The corrupted name and value are passed to hpack_dht_insert, where the truncated lengths are used to compute the dynamic table addresses and memcpy sizes, reaching the memory-safety sink.
